summary: A Network Host Status report from Ellen Westheimer of BBN covering March 13 to March 24, 1972. It lists which hosts were left out of daily testing, and notes that the SRI-AI computer became a server during the period. It updates RFC 319. It was replaced by RFC 330.

plainLanguage.summary: This is like a school attendance sheet for the early internet. Someone wrote down which big computers were switched on and ready to help, and which ones were not, so people knew where to go.

questions: what did arpanet host status codes mean
subtitle: A 1972 status report on which ARPANET hosts were up, and which were left out of daily testing.

tldr.problem: Network users needed to know which hosts were available as servers and which were reachable at all.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts daily from its Terminal IMP between March 13 and March 24, then published tables of each host's expected status and the daily results.
tldr.outcome: It records that SRI-AI became a server in that period. It updates RFC 319 and was obsoleted by RFC 330.

today: RFC 326 was obsoleted by RFC 330 and updated RFC 319. It is a snapshot of one two-week period in 1972.

sections.title: Scope of the Report
sections.content:
The report covers the status of most Network Hosts from March 13 to March 24. During this period the SRI-AI computer became a server.

Some hosts were excluded from the daily testing. One group was not expected to function as servers on a regular basis for at least two weeks, including MIT-AI (address 134) and Case (address 13), both PDP-10s.
sections.plainLanguage: The report says which computers were checked every day and which were skipped, like roll call with a few kids marked as away.

sections.title: Users-Only Hosts and Status Table
sections.content:
The second excluded group was hosts intended to be users only: the Terminal IMPs (AMES, MITRE, NBS, ETAC and BBN), the Network Control Center computer at address 5, which only gathers statistics, and four other hosts: Rand IBM-360/65, Harvard PDP-1, Illinois PDP-11 and NBS PDP-11.

A table lists each host by address, site and computer, with a status or prediction such as Server, User Only, Soon or June, and the person it was obtained from.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers were only for people to sit at, not for helping others. The table says what each one was doing or when it would be ready.

sections.title: Daily Test Results
sections.content:
A second table shows results for ten test times from 3/13 to 3/24, tested from the BBN Terminal IMP. Each cell is one letter: O Open, H half open (the host opened a connection then closed it or went silent), D Dead (dead or inaccessible), R Refused, and T Timed out (no completed ICP and open connection within 60 seconds).

The UCLA IBM-360/91 offers only a Network Job Service (NETRJS), which the Terminal IMP could not test, so a connection to the NETRJS logger was assumed to mean NETRJS worked.
sections.plainLanguage: Every day someone knocked on each computer's door. The letters say whether it answered, answered then went quiet, or never came to the door.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: 1/2 Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection but then closed it, or did not respond further.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: ICP and connection not completed within 60 seconds.

references.text: RFC 319, the report that this RFC updates.
